title: Commission starts enforcing AI Act rules and new transparency requirements on 2 August
key_claim: From 2 August 2026 the AI Office and national authorities begin enforcing the AI Act, and new transparency rules require interactive AI systems to disclose they are AI and AI-generated content to carry machine-readable marks.
frame_summary: Argues that the binding EU intervention this cycle is disclosure and labelling of AI output to the human reader; it makes no claim about how AI systems acquire input content, and does not concede that question to any other venue.
verbatim_quote: On the same date, new transparency rules will start to apply, requiring certain AI systems to tell users when they are interacting with AI and when content has been generated or altered by it.
notes: Tier 1 anchor for the argument that the binding EU instrument this cycle addresses output transparency, leaving the input-access question to private infrastructure. title: Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
key_claim: The government proposes not to intervene in the AI content licensing market at this stage, and will instead monitor market-led approaches to licensing as they develop.
frame_summary: Argues that copyright law is already adequate and that the licensing market should be allowed to form on its own terms, with government monitoring rather than legislating; non-intervention is presented as the right policy, not as an abdication.
verbatim_quote: The market for licensing copyright works for use with AI (artificial intelligence) technology is still new and evolving. We propose not to intervene in the licensing market at this stage.
notes: Single permitted structural anchor in the 3-6 month band. Canonical statement of the government-abstention position that leaves the field to infrastructure operators; also carries the counter-argument. title: Same gatekeepers, new tollbooths in the AI content licensing market
date_evidence:
Courtney C. Radsch Nonresident Fellow - Governance Studies, Center for Technology Innovation (CTI)

June 9, 2026
key_claim: Deal structures, price precedents, intermediary take rates and governance norms now being established will be difficult to dislodge once normalised, and the same firms eroding publisher traffic are building the licensing infrastructure publishers must use.
frame_summary: Argues that the AI content market is repeating the platform-capture pattern of the search and social eras, and that the window for policy intervention closes once commercial norms calcify.
verbatim_quote: The deal structures, price precedents, intermediary take rates, and governance norms being established right now will be difficult to dislodge once they’re normalized.
notes: Tier 2 spine source for the calcification argument. Author co-wrote the Open Markets Institute report the piece discusses; Brookings discloses Google and Microsoft as unrestricted donors. publisher: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism
title: Overview and key findings of the 2026 Digital News Report
key_claim: Weekly use of AI chatbots for news rose from 7% to 10% globally, and 42% of chatbot news users say they always or often click through to original sources.
frame_summary: Argues that AI chatbot news use is growing steadily rather than explosively, and that the onward-journey question for publishers is empirically open rather than settled.
verbatim_quote: Overall, 42% of AI chatbot users for news say they always or often click through from chatbot answers to original news sources but there are wide variations by market. Clicking through is most popular in South Korea (56%), more than twice the reported click-through behaviour in Denmark (26%). Propensity for clicking through from AI chatbots seems to sit between likelihood of clicking through from social media (36%) and search (44%), but these numbers should be compared with caution because they are proportions of quite different user bases.
verbatim_list: At the global level, weekly news usage has increased by 3pp from 7% to 10% of all audiences.
Our data this year show fast rather than explosive growth in the use of AI chatbots for news.
notes: Tier 2 demand-side anchor. Also supplies the counter-argument that answer-engine substitution is not yet mass behaviour. title: Towards an Agent-First Web: Redesigning the Web for AI Agents
key_claim: Between July 2025 and January 2026 the number of websites actively blocking AI crawlers was nearly seven times the number blocking traditional search crawlers such as Googlebot.
frame_summary: Argues that the web's open-access model has already failed empirically for agent traffic and that the technical architecture of access is the leverage point that needs redesigning, without claiming infrastructure operators should be the ones setting commercial terms.

title: Cloudflare's new policy pushes AI companies to pay for publishers' content
key_claim: From 15 September 2026 Cloudflare's default settings block mixed-use crawlers from any pages that host ads, applying to new customers, new sites set up by existing customers and all existing free customers.
frame_summary: Argues that a private infrastructure operator has set an industry deadline that forces AI companies to separate search crawling from training and agent access, or lose default access.
verbatim_quote: Starting on September 15, 2026, Cloudflare’s default settings will block “mixed-use” crawlers from any pages that host ads, the company announced on Wednesday.
verbatim_list: Cloudflare’s data suggested that over 50% of crawl traffic from AI crawlers is spent re-fetching unchanged pages
To put this into action, Cloudflare is initially working with two partners, Ceramic.ai and You.com.

title: Cloudflare says bot blocking is fuelling publisher AI deals
key_claim: Cloudflare, used by 20% of websites worldwide, says creating reliable scarcity through blocking is producing licensing deals, and it is shifting its default position from pay-per-crawl to pay-per-use.
frame_summary: Argues that engineered scarcity at the network edge, not litigation or regulation, is what has moved AI companies to the negotiating table with publishers.
verbatim_quote: Cloudflare said it will now shift its default position to “pay-per-use”, which is still at a very early stage, so publishers receive compensation if their content is surfaced in AI answers or otherwise directly creates value.
verbatim_list: Creating “reliable scarcity” by blocking companies from scraping content for AI uses is leading to more licensing revenue, according to internet hosting giant Cloudflare.
She said there are local news sites on Cloudflare’s network seeing a “path to having more licensing revenue than having ad revenue”.
notes: Freshest source in the set; carries the operator's own framing on scarcity and the pay-per-use pivot. title: The emerging AI content licensing market puts news publishers in a "double bind," a new report warns
key_claim: Intermediary take rates in the emerging licensing market vary widely: ScalePost takes roughly 15%, Cloudflare an estimated 30%, while TollBit and Sphere let publishers keep 100% and charge AI companies a transaction fee instead.
frame_summary: Argues that the intermediary layer forming between publishers and AI firms is capturing a material and unstandardised share of the revenue it brokers, and that this warrants regulatory scrutiny rather than being accepted as the settled market design.
verbatim_quote: A startup like ScalePost takes roughly a 15% cut of the revenue earned by “rights holders.” The authors estimate, based largely on interviews with stakeholders, that Cloudflare is taking about a 30% cut of revenue.
verbatim_list: Meanwhile, startups like TollBit and Sphere allow publishers to retain 100% of their revenue. Instead, they charge AI companies a separate transaction fee.
notes: Supplies the take-rate quantification anchor. Cut figures are the Open Markets Institute authors' estimates from stakeholder interviews, not disclosed rates.
